title: K-th Fastest Finisher
aka: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
story: At a city marathon, each finishing time in seconds is inserted into a binary search tree as the runner crosses the line: faster times go left, slower times go right. The tree is never re-sorted, so its shape depends on who finished when.

The prize table wants to call up runners by place: the 3rd fastest, then the 10th fastest for a random spot prize. You are given the tree and a place k. The tree already keeps the times in order, so there should be no need to copy them all out and sort them.
task: Write kthFastest(root, k). root is a valid binary search tree. Return the k-th smallest value in it, where k = 1 means the smallest.

All times are different, and k is always between 1 and the number of nodes. Trees are shown in level order, like [9000, 8000, 9500], where null marks a missing child. Your function receives real TreeNode objects with val, left and right.
constraints: The tree is a valid binary search tree, at most 500 levels deep.

examples.explanation: In order, the times are 7800, 8000, 8600, 9000, 9200, 9500, 9900. The 3rd is 8600. Reading the tree level by level would give 9000, 8000, 9500, so the 3rd value in the tree layout (9500) is the wrong answer.
With 7 runners, place 7 is the slowest: the rightmost node. Places count from 1, so k = 7 is the last, not past the end.

hints: In a search tree, where is the fastest time of all? And which time comes right after it?
Visiting the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree visits the values from smallest to largest. That order is called in-order.
So the answer is the k-th node an in-order walk visits. Do you need to finish the walk once you have counted to k?

Do an in-order walk with a counter (recursively, or with an explicit stack: push nodes while going left, pop one, count it, then go to its right child). When the counter reaches k, return that node's value and stop.
bruteForce: Collect every time into a list, sort it, and return the item at position k - 1. That is O(n log n) and it always visits all n runners, even when you only want the fastest.

The sort is wasted work: a binary search tree already stores the times in order, you just have to read them in the right order. An in-order walk lists them sorted for free and can stop after k of them.

walkthrough: In a binary search tree, everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is larger. So "left subtree, node, right subtree" visits the values in sorted order. Count as you visit and stop at k.
• Pop 7800. Count 1. It has no right child.
• Pop 8000. Count 2. Go to its right child 8600 and slide left: push 8600.
The walk never touched 9500, 9200 or 9900. The explicit stack does what the recursion stack would do, but makes it easy to stop the moment the count reaches k.
solution.timeWhy: You slide down at most h nodes to reach the smallest, then visit k nodes in order (each slide is paid for once).
solution.spaceWhy: The stack holds at most one path from the root, so at most h nodes.
solution.takeaway: An in-order walk of a binary search tree produces its values in sorted order. Whenever a question about a search tree mentions rank, order, "next larger" or "k-th", reach for in-order traversal and stop as soon as you have enough.
